title: Identification of Metal Oxide Nanoparticles in Histological Samples by Enhanced Darkfield Microscopy and Hyperspectral Mapping
protocol: Plug in and turn on the light source, XY stage controller, optical camera (for darkfield imaging), hyperspectral camera, and computer system.
Set the light source to 75% power.
Raise the stage to maximum height.
Connect the light guide to the condenser for enhanced darkfield imaging or to the collimator on the back of the microscope for reflected brightfield imaging.
Set the light source to 75% power for uniform illumination.
Raise the condenser to operating position.
Apply 3-5 drops of type-A immersion oil on the condenser lens carefully, avoiding bubbles.
Wipe away and reapply immersion oil if bubbles form.
Position the slide on the stage.
Slowly raise the condenser until the immersion oil contacts the slide.
Focus and align the condenser by examining through oculars.
Move the stage up and down via coarse objective focus knob to maximize brightness.
Move the condenser focus up and down via condenser adjustment knob to achieve maximum brightness.
Adjust condenser alignment knobs as necessary to center the bright spot.
Use fine objective focus knob to bring the bright spot into focus.
Readjust focus plane when changing objectives for different magnification.
Apply a drop of immersion oil over the coverslip when using 100X objective.
Use stage controller to find a region of interest.
Bring the region into focus using the fine objective focus knob.
Adjust the condenser focus as necessary to equilibrate illumination.
Determine what images or datacubes will be captured and in what sequence.
Open the optical imaging software.
Click on “Settings” in the menu bar.
Select the “Image Capture Button for capture event”.
Select the stored image format (TIFF was used for this experiment).
Assign a filename.
Browse and select a stored image folder.
Keep default timelapse.
Click “OK”.
Select exposure settings that create the highest contrast image (level of 0.0%, gain of 3.0 dB, shutter of 35 ms).
Capture the image by clicking the “Image” button in the menu bar.
Capture several low-magnification darkfield images by changing the microscope objectives.
Provide context for high magnification images with additional low-magnification images.
Capture optical images at the same magnification as any datacubes that will be captured with the hyperspectral camera.
Ensure consistent magnification for all datacubes to maintain accuracy of spectral angle mapper (SAM).
Redirect light source knob on the microscope to the hyperspectral camera.
Minimize but do not close the optical imaging software window.
Open hyperspectral imaging software for acquisition of HSI datacubes.
Select “Hyperspectral Microscope” in the menu bar.
Choose “HSI Microscope Controls”.
Set the objective magnification.
Specify the save path for files.
Adjust the field of view or number of lines in settings (use 720 lines).
Set the exposure time to 0.25 seconds.
Preview HSI and adjust fine objective focus to sharpen peaks in the preview image.
If focusing with the preview is difficult, switch to optical imaging software.
Focus using the optical camera’s focal length adjustment slider.
Return to hyperspectral imaging software after focusing.
Shift the slide bar back to the hyperspectral camera.
Adjust source brightness or condenser focus to preview intensity between 1,000 and 16,000 units.
Cancel preview to adjust exposure time if necessary.
Click "capture" to start imaging process.
Take a dark current image by adjusting the upper slide bar or aperture carefully.
Restore the slide bar or aperture to its correct position after taking the dark current image.
Wait for the progress indicator to complete before disturbing the scope.
Observe four new windows: “Available bands list”, “#1zoom”, “#1scroll”, and “#1 RGB band”.
Maximize the “#1RGB band” window for future datacube references.
Right click the datacube and save it as a TIFF.
Click “OK”.
If imaging is finished, put away all samples.
Clean all oil-exposed surfaces with 70% isopropanol in water.
Raise stage to maximum height.
Lower condenser to minimum height and press into non-operational position.
Shut down or unplug the light source.
Shut down or unplug the stage controller.
Shut down or unplug the cameras.
Right click in the image window.
Left click "Z-profile spectrum".
Left click onto pixels of interest on the datacube, particularly the brightest ones or those that can be confidently identified as representing the material of interest.
Observe the Spectral Profile window showing the associated spectrum.
Take note of their lowest and highest value and which wavelength corresponds to it.
Survey the positive control sample by clicking the regions of interest that are very bright relative to the surrounding tissue, especially those with readily identifiable particles.
Use the “Particle Filter” tool under the “Particle Analysis” menu to identify particles present in the datacube.
In the new pop-up window, observe the “Spectral Max Must Exceed” value.
Set this value so it is higher than background pixels but lower than the materials of interest.
Leave other parameters to default.
Adjust the “Size Threshold” box to exclude objects based on size.
Set Spectral Max Must Exceed to 5,000.
Set Valid Data Max to 16,000.
Set Size Threshold (pixels) to 400.
Click “OK” after setting all parameters.
Observe the resulting graph with details of particles detected within the indicated intensity threshold.
Export the data if characteristic maximum reflectance wavelength is known and select particles with a similar “Max WL” value.
Select all particles for export if the maximum reflectance wavelength is unknown.
Click “Export”; “To Spectral Library”.
Choose a file name then click “OK”.
Select a sample that will serve as a negative control.
Ensure the negative control was prepared and treated in the same way as experimental samples but without nanoparticles of interest.
Guarantee the absence of nanoparticles similar or identical to the material of interest in the negative control.
Use porcine skin not exposed to metal oxide nanomaterials for negative controls.
Obtain several datacubes from the negative control using the hyperspectral camera.
Filter the spectral library collected for the positive control against each datacube captured for the negative controls serially.
Click “Filter Spectral Library” under the Analysis menu in the hyperspectral imaging software.
Open the spectral library created for the positive control as the Input file.
Select “Image” under the Spectral Data box for external source.
Keep default settings under the Processing Parameters box.
Choose an Output Name For Filtered Library that is different from the original spectral library name.
Click “OK” to proceed with filtering.
Open and select the first datacube captured in step 3.2.2 for the negative control as a source image.
Open the “Spectral Angle Mapper” from the hyperspectral imaging software.
Select the experimental datacube in the pop-up window and click “OK”.
If no file names are listed, open a new file, choose the experimental datacube, then click “OK”.
Click “Import” in the Endmember Collection:SAM menu bar.
Select “from Spectral Library file” to import the reference spectral library created in step 3.2.3.
Click “Select All Items” in the Input Spectral Library window and click “OK”.
Right-click on “Color” and select “Apply default colors to all.”
Click “Select all,” followed by “Apply.”
Choose the output file name and click “OK”.
Open the datacube in the hyperspectral imaging software.
Select “Classification” in the Overlay menu of the image window.
Navigate to the file name and click “OK”.
Select the “Merge Classes” option from the Option menu in the “Interactive class tool” opened through the Overlay menu.
Highlight all classifications to combine, typically everything except “unclassified” in the “classes to merge into base” list.
Select a single spectrum from the “base class” list and click “OK”.
Click on the color selected to show matching spectra in that color.
Click on the “unclassified” colors box to obtain a dichromatic image with matching spectra over a black background.
Right click to save the image as a TIFF, including any overlays currently active.
Select "Class Distribution" from the Option menu in the "Interactive Class Tool" window.
Acquire mapping statistics for unmapped pixels and classified materials.
Open hyperspectral mapped images in NIH ImageJ software.
Use the Image menu, Adjust submenu, “Threshold” function to differentiate particles of interest.
Set threshold parameters: default method, color red, HSB color space, dark background, hue, saturation, brightness checkboxes checked.
Generate an image by unifying relevant classes and overlaying with unclassified colors.
Use the Analyze menu and select “Analyze particles” function.
Set the parameters as follows: size 0-infinity, circularity 0-1, show nothing.
Check the display results checkbox.
Export the data to another software program for statistical comparison with control samples.
Copy the data displayed in the results table after step 4.2.4 to a spreadsheet.
Use the MAX function on the first (untitled) column to determine the number of particles.
Use the AVERAGE function on the Area column to determine mean size of a particle.
